comm.t: The outer narrator takes over again. Medhas’s teaching is finished; Mārkaṇḍeya, telling the whole story to his own listener (addressed as महामुने in 13.9), now reports what the king and the merchant did.

mantras.anvaya_en: An absolutive phrase and the subject; the main verb follows in 13.9 after the further absolutive प्रणिपत्य (13.8).
mantras.lit: Having heard his words thus, Suratha, that lord of men —
mantras.tr: When Suratha, lord of men, had heard the seer’s words,
mantras.tr_note: The sentence continues through 13.8 to its verb in 13.9.

comm.t: A half-verse of transition. The long dialogue that began in 1.39 is over; from here the story moves quickly to action.

samasa.type: prādi tatpuruṣa (a tatpuruṣa whose first member is the prefix अति)
samasa.sense: by his overgrown attachment to what he called his own
samasa.alt: अति could also be read as a separate adverb with निर्विण्णः (‘utterly disenchanted by attachment’); the written text is the same. The compound fits the teaching, which is about ममत्व itself (1.41, 1.53).

samasa.literal: by the carrying-off of the kingdom
samasa.sense: by the loss of his throne (1.6–9)

morph.note: Absolutive in -य (ल्यप्), used when the root has a prefix. The n of नि becomes ṇ after the r of प्र (internal retroflexion).
Past participle of निर् + √विद् ‘to be weary of, disgusted with’: the suffix -न (not -त) and the retroflex ṇṇ (विद् + न → विण्ण). Its cause stands in the instrumental.
ममत्व, an abstract noun in -त्व built on the pronoun मम ‘my’: ‘the state of saying “mine”’.

mantras.anvaya: (सः सुरथः) अतिममत्वेन राज्यापहरणेन च निर्विण्णः, महाभागं शंसितव्रतं तम् ऋषिं प्रणिपत्य (13.9: … जगाम)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A second absolutive (प्रणिपत्य) with its object, and a participle (निर्विण्णः) with two instrumentals of cause, all describing the subject of 13.7.
mantras.lit: — having bowed down to that greatly blessed seer of praiseworthy vows, weary through his excessive sense of ‘mine’ and the seizure of his kingdom —
mantras.tr: bowed low before that illustrious seer, so steadfast in his vows. Sick at heart from his own clinging and from the loss of his kingdom,
mantras.tr_note: The participial phrase is rendered as a separate clause; the sentence still runs on to 13.9.

comm.t: The king bows to his teacher and goes. Two causes of his weariness are named together: the inner one (excessive ममत्व, the sense of ‘mine’) and the outer one (the loss of the kingdom). The first is what the teaching diagnosed (1.41: ममत्वं गतराज्यस्य).
A modern reading: the verse puts the private cause before the public one. Suratha’s grief came less from what he had lost than from how tightly he had held it.

samasa.sense: Mārkaṇḍeya’s address to his own listener

samasa.type: caturthī tatpuruṣa with अर्थ (a compound that is always formed), used adverbially
samasa.sense: in order to behold the Mother

samasa.type: saptamī tatpuruṣa (its first member नदीपुलिन is a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa: नद्याः पुलिनम्)
samasa.literal: staying on the sandbank of a river
samasa.sense: settled on a river shore for his austerity

morph.note: Perfect of √गम्: reduplicated ज-गाम (the reduplicated g becomes j), with the strong vowel ā in the third person singular. The singular verb takes the king as its subject and adds the merchant (स च वैश्यः) as a second.
Dative of purpose (तादर्थ्य): ‘(he went) for austerity’.

mantras.anvaya: (सुरथः) सद्यः तपसे जगाम, सः वैश्यः च, महामुने। अम्बायाः संदर्शनार्थं नदीपुलिनसंस्थितः (अभवत्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main verb जगाम completes the sentence of 13.7–8. Its subject is Suratha; the merchant is added with च. The second line gives the purpose (संदर्शनार्थम्) and the place (नदीपुलिनसंस्थितः).
mantras.lit: — went at once to austerity, and that merchant too, O great sage; for the sake of seeing the Mother, staying on the sandbank of a river.
mantras.tr: he went at once to practise austerity, great sage, and the merchant with him. To behold the Mother, they settled on the sandy bank of a river.
mantras.tr_note: The singular participle नदीपुलिनसंस्थितः is rendered with ‘they’, since both men stay on the river bank (13.10: तौ तस्मिन् पुलिने).

comm.t: The king and the merchant leave at once for austerity. Their purpose is stated plainly: to see the Mother (अम्बा). The vocative महामुने is Mārkaṇḍeya’s address to his own listener — a reminder that the whole story is being told inside the Purāṇa’s frame.
The river bank (पुलिन) is a classic place of tapas: open, quiet and near water for the rites. The Devī Māhātmya does not name the river.

flags.uncertain: नदीपुलिनसंस्थितः is singular although both men stay on the bank; it is read with the nearest subject (or with each). The listener addressed as महामुने is, in the Purāṇa’s frame, Krauṣṭuki (see 1.1).

samasa.sense: a hymn in praise of the Goddess, used for japa

morph.note: Perfect of √तप् in the ātmanepada. With तपस् as its object the root takes middle endings (a rule of Pāṇini’s for this phrase); the reduplicated ta-tap- contracts to tep- before the weak perfect endings, as in पेचे from √पच्.
Taddhita -मय (मयट्) ‘made of’: महीमय ‘made of earth’. मयट् forms its feminine in -ī: महीमयी.
Present participle in the nominative: the recitation accompanies the austerity.

mantras.anvaya: सः च वैश्यः (च) परं देवीसूक्तं जपन् तपः तेपे। तौ तस्मिन् पुलिने देव्याः महीमयीं मूर्तिं कृत्वा (13.11: … अर्हणां चक्रतुः)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is complete: two subjects with a singular verb and a participle of accompanying action. The second line begins a new sentence whose verb is in 13.11.
mantras.lit: And he and the merchant practised austerity, reciting the supreme Devīsūkta. The two, having made on that sandbank an earthen image of the Goddess —
mantras.tr: There the king and the merchant practised austerities, chanting the supreme hymn to the Goddess. On that sandbank they shaped an image of the Goddess out of clay,
mantras.tr_note: सः ‘he’ is rendered ‘the king’. The sentence of the second line is completed in 13.11.

comm.t: The worship begins: austerity, recitation of a hymn, and an image of the Goddess made from the earth of the river bank. Everything they use is at hand; nothing is bought or brought.

Which hymn is meant by देवीसूक्त is debated in the tradition. One view identifies it with the Vedic Devīsūkta (Ṛgveda 10.125, the hymn of Vāk) recited with the Saptaśatī; another with the hymn of the gods in chapter 5 (5.9 ff., नमो देव्यै महादेव्यै), which the pāṭha tradition also calls a Devīsūkta. The text itself does not say.
A modern reading: the image is made of the same earth on which they sit. The Goddess they seek is worshipped first in the most ordinary material there is.

flags.uncertain: स च वैश्यः is read ‘he (the king) and the merchant’, with the singular verb agreeing with the nearest subject (both men worship in the next line: तौ). It can also be read ‘and that merchant too (practised austerity)’, the king’s austerity being already stated in 13.9; the meaning of the scene is the same.
